summary:
MissionLens is an interactive web platform developed by Team JupyLab to make NASA's abandoned space exploration hardware more accessible and interesting to young learners.

We developed a digital experience featuring five space exploration missions: Apollo 15, Viking 1, Voyager 1, Opportunity, and Ingenuity. Through engaging mission stories, narrated explanations, interactive 3D hardware models, videos, and links to NASA resources, users can explore the machines behind these missions and understand their designs, functions, and contributions to space exploration.

MissionLens addresses the Abandoned but Not Forgotten challenge by bringing attention to space exploration equipment whose missions have ended but whose scientific and engineering value remains. Rather than leaving learners to navigate scattered technical articles and complex explanations, we bring relevant information together in an accessible, visual, and interactive experience.

We believe that when young people understand the engineering behind space exploration, they are more likely to develop curiosity about science, technology, and future space missions. A mission may end, but the knowledge it leaves behind should never be forgotten.
details:
MissionLens: Stories from the Edge of Discovery is an interactive, Bilingual educational web platform developed by Team JupyLab in response to NASA's Abandoned but Not Forgotten challenge. Our goal is to preserve the educational value of completed space missions by making their technology, engineering, and stories accessible to the next generation.

The platform features five space exploration missions: Apollo 15's Lunar Rover, Viking 1, Voyager 1, Opportunity, and Ingenuity. Rather than presenting scattered technical information, MissionLens organizes these missions into short, chronological stories that guide users through the different machines, their purposes, and their contributions to space exploration.

How does it work?

MissionLens combines four major learning experiences:

- Interactive storytelling: Users explore five carefully structured mission stories, presented in a chronological sequence. The stories are concise, visually engaging, and available in both English and French. Users can also download stories to read offline, making educational content accessible to learners in rural communities and areas with limited or unreliable internet connectivity.

- Audio narration: Recognizing that not everyone enjoys reading or learns best through text, we incorporated audio narration across the stories. Users can listen to the explanations while following the content, providing an alternative and more engaging way to learn.

- Interactive 3D Hardware Lab: Users can explore 3D models of actual space exploration hardware, rotating and examining the machines to understand their structures and components. This offers a more hands-on experience than simply viewing photographs.

- Video and NASA Resources: Users can watch relevant mission footage and access links to trusted NASA resources for further exploration and learning.

What makes MissionLens unique?

Our unique value proposition lies in combining accessibility, storytelling, and hands-on exploration in one platform. We considered that learners have different preferences, resources, and learning environments. Some prefer reading, others listening, while others learn better through visual interaction. MissionLens accommodates these differences through downloadable stories, bilingual content, audio narration, videos, and interactive 3D models.

The offline-download feature is particularly important to us. We recognize that internet access is not equally available everywhere, especially in rural communities. Allowing users to download stories means they can continue learning even when they are not connected to the internet.

Our chronological storytelling approach also makes the experience more structured, helping users follow the missions rather than navigate disconnected pieces of information.

Technology and development tools

We developed MissionLens using:

  • HTML for structuring the website.
  • CSS for styling and visual presentation.
  • JavaScript for interactive functionality.
  • React for building the website's user interface and components.
  • Visual Studio Code with AI-assisted coding tools to support development, code generation, and debugging. The team retained responsibility for the implementation and integration of the code.
  • Replit as part of our development workflow.
  • Netlify for hosting and deploying the website.

We also sourced authentic mission imagery and footage from NASA's Image and Video Library and obtained 3D hardware models from NASA's 3D Resources GitHub repository.

Intended impact and future development

We want MissionLens to make space exploration more accessible, encourage curiosity about aerospace engineering, and inspire young people to pursue science, technology, engineering, and mathematics.

We also recognize that our current version is a developing prototype, not a finished product. Our next steps include expanding the language options beyond English and French, adding more missions, introducing quizzes and interactive learning activities, improving the 3D experience, and conducting user testing to understand how young learners interact with the platform.

Ultimately, we want to demonstrate that the end of a space mission should never mean the end of its educational value.
